fit: self-reported visual complaints in Parkinson disease
assessment: The systematic review compiles patient-reported visual complaints across studies and distinguishes them from functional visual tests. It documents heterogeneity in phenotyping and does not identify an intake comparison using dried figs or a defined change in visual episode frequency after food.

fit: longitudinal plasma pTau181 and clinical visual symptom ratings
assessment: The cohort compares biomarker trajectories across mild cognitive impairment with Lewy bodies and Alzheimer categories and applies the North-East Visual Hallucinations Inventory. Ratings are higher in probable Lewy body cases than in the Alzheimer-type group. The later plasma paper reuses pTau181 measurements. Neither gives a dried fig intervention or food-timed visual episodes.

fit: 36-month follow-up of a small Parkinson dementia stimulation trial
assessment: Five of six participants from the earlier basal forebrain stimulation trial enter long-term follow-up. Individual NPI hallucination scores include improvement, no change and worsening. This open longitudinal phase reuses the 2017 crossover cohort and has no dried fig exposure.

fit: donepezil challenge, withdrawal and re-exposure in two dementia cases
assessment: Two original cases report complex hallucinations around donepezil exposure. One describes cessation after withdrawal, and the other recurrence after re-exposure. These are medication time courses in dementia with no dried fig contrast or Parkinson visual episode assessment.

fit: 5-HT3 antagonist effects on sensory measures and psychosis
assessment: The human-study review compares sensory processing and pharmacologic evidence and cites earlier uncontrolled ondansetron reports in Parkinson hallucinosis. It identifies the ongoing TOP HAT trial as separate. Neither medicine nor the reviews establish a dried fig exposure or episode result after food.

fit: sham-controlled basal forebrain stimulation and individual clinical visual observations
assessment: Six Parkinson disease dementia participants complete a double-blind crossover of active versus sham stimulation. The primary cognitive measures did not consistently improve. The exploratory total Neuropsychiatric Inventory contrast favored active treatment by a median five points versus sham (95% CI 2.5–8.5). Two participants reported near-cessation of visual hallucinations while stimulation was active and resurgence after it was turned off. This is the registered NCT01701544 intervention and the parent cohort of the 36-month report PMC9346244. The trial does not test food intake.

fit: selected severe hypomagnesemia case synthesis and visual outcome citation boundaries
assessment: The review identifies 60 patients with neurological symptoms during hypomagnesemia. Inclusion required movement or eye movement abnormalities and clinical reversal following correction. The resulting series cannot estimate the probability of improvement without that selection, or a visual hallucination treatment effect. References 41 and 42 describe hallucinations without specifying the sensory modality in the original cases. Reference 4 remains at publisher preview depth. Do not count this synthesis as additional independent case evidence. It contains no dried fig feeding or Parkinson episode-frequency comparison.

fit: nighttime hallucinations during a recurrent severe magnesium depletion case
assessment: Initial ataxia and vertigo improved during intravenous magnesium replacement. Three months later, nighttime hallucinations of unspecified modality were reported with recurrent motor symptoms and a measured serum magnesium concentration of 0.9 mg/dL. Overall symptoms improved during repeat replacement and proton pump inhibitor cessation. The original does not separately quantify hallucination resolution, frequency, or a Parkinson or dietary fig exposure.

fit: delirium hallucinations of unreported modality during magnesium and calcium disturbance
assessment: Page 168 lists delirium with hallucinations during a period of neurologic deterioration, with no modality or episode rate. Clinical signs and electrolyte abnormalities improved overall during intravenous magnesium treatment. Table 1 on page 169 reports serum magnesium of 0.42 mEq/L before and 1.48 mEq/L after infusion. The later clinical follow-up records changes in serum electrolytes and drug exposure. It does not separately track visual episodes. The NLM electronic date is May 20, 2010, and the printed note says May 21. There is no Parkinson or dried fig exposure in the case.

fit: registered 12-week hallucination scale comparison without posted outcomes
assessment: TOP HAT registers an ondansetron-versus-placebo comparison with a hallucination endpoint at 12 weeks. The sponsor describes the SAPS hallucinations score as assessing frequency or severity. The official registry does not supply results. This prescription trial is separate from food exposure and earlier uncontrolled case series.
